'''Harry Soodak''' (December 24, 1920 &ndash; September 30, 2008) was an American physicist who worked on the [[Manhattan Project]], publishing the first design of a sodium-cooled [[breeder reactor]], and was a professor at [[City College of New York]]. Along with [[Arthur Iberall]], Soodak developed the concept of [[homeokinetics]] to explain the functioning of complex systems.

==Biography==
Soodak was born in [[New York City]].  Married to Martha for 55 years, they had three children Deborah, Robert, and Lenore.<ref name=HSobit>[http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/nytimes/obituary.aspx?n=harry-soodak&pid=118392594#sthash.IlANt6tm.dpuf New York Times obituary]</ref>

Soodak received his bachelor's degree from the [[City College of New York]] (CCNY) in February 1940, a master's degree from [[Columbia University]], and his Ph.D. from [[Duke University]] in 1944.<ref name=PhysicsToday>[http://scitation.aip.org/content/aip/magazine/physicstoday/news/10.1063/PT.4.2047 Physics Today]</ref>

Soodak worked on the [[Manhattan Project]] at [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]] where he gave courses on nuclear physics and reactor theory.  According to Oak Ridge Director [[Alvin M. Weinberg]], these courses were "phenomenally successful" and Soodak had the reputation in the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission]] of being "one of the clearest lecturers in the business.”<ref name= PhysicsToday /> In 1945, Harry and [[Eugene Wigner]] published the first design of a sodium-cooled [[breeder reactor]].<ref name= PhysicsToday />  Following work at the Manhattan Project, he served as a research associate at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] for nearly three years.  In 1949, Soodak joined the physics department of his alma mater, [[City College of New York]].  He retired in 1992.<ref name= PhysicsToday />

==Contributions==
Soodak signed the July 13, 1945 addendum to the [[Szilard petition]] that asked that the Japanese be given the opportunity to surrender before bombing them.<ref>[http://www.dannen.com/decision/oakridge1.html Addendum to Szilard petition]</ref> Commenting on Soodak's early work, as well as his continuing contributions to nuclear physics after coming to CCNY – which included lecturing on nuclear theory in the graduate schools of NYU and of Columbia – [[Mark W. Zemansky]], who was then chairman of the physics department at CCNY, wrote in 1958: "During the war, Dr. Soodak made a name for himself in the field of reactor design. Through his theoretical work, in books and articles, and his practical applications, he has become a leading international authority on the design of nuclear reactors. There is hardly a handbook or treatise to which he has not contributed or served in an editorial capacity."<ref name= PhysicsToday />  Without doubt Harry Soodak's greatest legacy is the decisive influence he had on the hundreds of undergraduate students he taught and advised at CCNY.<ref name=PhysicsToday />

In the 1970s, Soodak began working with [[Arthur Iberall]] in an area of [[complex systems]]. They were observing an area that physics has neglected, that of complex systems with their very long internal factory day delays.<ref>Soodak H. and A.S. Iberall. Homeokinetics: A physical science for complex systems. Science 201:579, 1978.</ref><ref>Iberall, A.S., H. Soodak and C. Arensberg. Homeokinetic physics of societies - A new discipline: Autonomous groups, cultures, polities. In: H. Reul, Ghista, D., and Rau, G. (eds.). Perspectives in Biomechanics, Vol. I, Part A. Harwood Academic Press, N.Y., pp. 433–527, 1980.</ref><ref>Iberall, A. and Soodak, H.: A physics for complex systems. In: F. Yates, (ed.), Self-Organizing Systems, pp. 499–520. Plenum Press, NY 1987, p 499-520.</ref><ref>Soodak, H., Iberall, A. Thermodynamics and complex systems. In: F.E. Yates, (ed.). Self-Organizing Systems: The Emergence of Order. New York: Plenum Press, 1987, p 459-469.</ref> These systems are associated with nested hierarchy and with an extensive range of time scale processes. It was such connections, referred to as both up-down or in-out connections (as nested [[hierarchy]]) and side-side or flatland physics among atomistic-like components (as [[heterarchy]]) that became the hallmark of homeokinetic problems. By 1975, they began to describe [[homeokinetics]], the physics of complex, self-organizing systems, as dealing with the problems of nature, life, humankind, mind, and society.<ref>2016. Iberall, Arthur S., Homeokinetics: The Basics, Medfield, MA: Strong Voices Publishing, {{ISBN|978-0-990-53614-7}}</ref>

The Harry Soodak Memorial Scholarship at the CCNY Physics Department was created in his honor.<ref>[https://www.ccny.cuny.edu/sites/default/files/PhysicsAwards2.pdf Harry Soodak Memorial Scholarship]</ref>
